name: Tempo code training (3/1/4/2)

card.summary: Tempo code training sets the duration of each phase of a lift (for example 3 seconds lowering, 1 pause, 4 lifting, 2 at the top) to control muscle tension for physique-building.

quick.overview:
A tempo code such as 3/1/4/2 gives the seconds for each phase of a repetition: lowering, pause at the bottom, lifting, and pause at the top. Lifters use tempos to control how long muscles stay under load.

The appearance chain is training to build muscle and a better physique. Research on tempo and muscle growth is mixed: Wikipedia summarises studies where slow and normal speeds both increased muscle, and concludes total volume and progressive overload matter more than rep speed alone.
quick.how: Lifters write the four numbers next to an exercise and count them through each rep. Moderate tempos of roughly 2 to 8 seconds per phase are described in the literature; very slow tempos can limit the load that can be lifted.
quick.risks: No special risks beyond ordinary resistance training; slower tempos reduce the weight usable, which affects progression.

lead: Tempo code training prescribes the duration of each phase of a lift using a four-number code such as 3/1/4/2. Wikipedia describes tempo as the time a muscle spends under tension each rep, adjustable by slowing the lowering or lifting phase or pausing at points in the movement.[1]
People use it in hypertrophy training to build muscle for a larger or more defined physique. Proposed benefits are that slower tempos raise muscle activity and so promote growth.[1]
Research is mixed: Burd and colleagues (2012) found higher protein synthesis with slow reps at light loads, while Schuenke and colleagues (2012) found the biggest gains in a normal-speed group.[1]

chain: Set phase durations for each rep
Control time under tension and form
Supports consistent training toward muscle growth
angle.text: Tempo is a training variable. Lifters use it to shape how each set is performed in pursuit of more muscle.

infobox: Eccentric / bottom pause / concentric / top pause

paras: The four numbers refer to the lowering phase, the pause at the bottom, the lifting phase and the pause at the top. Wikipedia notes that very fast tempos shorten time under tension while very slow ones limit load.[1]

The literature cited by Wikipedia points to moderate tempos around 2 to 8 seconds per phase, and concludes that long-term hypertrophy depends more on total volume and progressive overload than repetition duration.[1]

Two small studies are summarised in Wikipedia: Burd et al. (2012) measured acute protein synthesis with 6-second slow versus 1-second fast reps at light loads, and Schuenke et al. (2012) compared slow and normal-speed training in untrained participants.[1] No study of the specific 3/1/4/2 code was found.
